paragraphs: Testing pairs of gene perturbations can reveal interactions useful for combination therapies, but the number of possible pairs makes exhaustive screening impractical. NAIAD addresses this experimental selection problem: it learns from available measurements and recommends gene pairs predicted to produce the strongest effects, helping direct subsequent experiments toward promising combinations.

The framework combines information about individual gene perturbations with adaptive gene embeddings. These learned representations scale with the amount of training data. This design addresses two competing needs: limiting overfitting when few combinations have been measured and representing more complicated gene interactions as additional observations become available.

The authors evaluate NAIAD on four CRISPR datasets containing more than 350,000 interactions. With small training datasets, it outperforms existing models by up to 40%, and its recommendations accelerate discovery with fewer experiments. They also extend the approach to selecting drug combinations from 2,000 candidates. These findings support using adaptive prediction to guide combinatorial screening, with the reported improvement representing the upper end of the observed gains.
icml-2025-active-learning-for-efficient-.tldr: NAIAD adapts its gene representations as data grows to identify promising gene and drug combinations with fewer experiments.

paragraphs: Generating graphs requires learning distributions over relational structures. Graph diffusion models perform well at this task, but their training procedures tightly constrain how samples are produced. DeFoG separates these stages, creating more freedom to choose sampling procedures that improve generation quality or require fewer successive refinement steps.

The framework uses discrete flow matching while respecting graph symmetries. Its theoretical contribution connects the training objective to the sampling algorithm despite their separation, and establishes that the formulation reproduces the target graph distribution. This connection matters because greater freedom in sampling still needs a mathematical relationship to what the model learned during training.

The authors explore this design space and introduce sampling methods that improve performance while reducing refinement steps. Experiments span synthetic graphs, molecules, and digital pathology, with both unconditional and conditional generation. DeFoG achieves reported state-of-the-art results and outperforms most diffusion-based models using only 5–10% of their sampling steps. That comparison concerns the number of sampling steps; the abstract does not equate it with an identical reduction in runtime.
icml-2025-defog-discrete-flow-matching-f.tldr: DeFoG separates graph-generator training from sampling and outperforms most diffusion-based models using only 5–10% of their sampling steps.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks process information through the spectral structure of a graph Laplacian, a matrix representing graph connectivity. Repeated eigenvalues limit these networks' expressiveness. This paper addresses that limitation by changing the matrix underlying the model, making a richer set of distinct eigenvalues available for processing graph signals.

The authors construct a higher-dimensional sheaf Laplacian that encodes graph topology and raises the upper bound on the number of distinct eigenvalues. They obtain their perturbed sheaf Laplacian through carefully designed changes to a block representation of the normalized graph Laplacian. The construction therefore ties the added spectral diversity to a structured representation of the graph.

The theoretical analysis examines the expressiveness of networks using this matrix and bounds how the perturbations affect eigenvalues. Experiments on node-classification benchmarks show improved performance when the perturbed sheaf Laplacian is incorporated. Together, these results connect a specific spectral limitation to a concrete architectural modification: enriching the operator used to process graph signals can improve the tested models' ability to classify nodes.
icml-2025-enhancing-spectral-gnns-from-t.tldr: A perturbed sheaf Laplacian gives spectral graph neural networks richer spectral structure and improves node classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes successive decisions before all feedback from earlier decisions has arrived. Curvature in the loss functions can improve learning guarantees, but existing guarantees for strongly convex losses depend on the longest delay. The paper observes that this dependence can produce a worse bound than one based on the square root of total delay.

For strongly convex losses, the authors modify follow-the-regularized-leader to obtain a regret bound taking the smaller of two quantities: maximum outstanding observations times log T, and the square root of total delay. Here T is the time horizon. This allows the guarantee to reflect both the backlog of missing feedback and accumulated delay.

For exp-concave losses, an adaptive delayed Online Newton Step method similarly combines a curvature-sensitive bound with the square-root total-delay bound; its first term includes dimension and maximum delay. The authors also obtain a related guarantee for unconstrained online linear regression using a modified forecaster with clipping. Experiments across different losses and delay patterns report improved performance, supporting the practical relevance of adapting to more than the single longest delay.
icml-2025-exploiting-curvature-in-online.tldr: New online optimization algorithms combine curvature-sensitive guarantees with total-delay bounds to handle delayed feedback more effectively.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several sources of information, some of which may be missing for individual samples. Anchor-based methods make large datasets more manageable by representing relationships through a smaller set of anchors. FIML focuses on learning these anchors well while coordinating them with graph construction and the eventual clustering.

The method jointly learns a shared anchor graph, the anchors themselves, and a graph partition. Sharing the graph supports consistency across views, while adaptive weights balance how much each view contributes. FIML also connects the anchor graph to the similarity matrix used in symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization, giving graph entries an interpretation as similarities between anchors and original samples.

An alternating optimization procedure solves the combined problem. Bringing these stages into one framework allows anchor learning and clustering to be optimized together instead of treating the anchor graph as a fixed intermediate result. Experiments on multiple incomplete multi-view datasets report better clustering performance than comparison methods. The contribution is an integrated approach to scalable clustering when different samples provide different subsets of the available views.
icml-2025-fast-incomplete-multi-view-clu.tldr: FIML jointly learns anchors, a shared graph, and clusters to improve scalable clustering when samples have missing views.

paragraphs: Blind face restoration reconstructs a high-quality face image from an input affected by unknown degradation. Many diffusion methods guide restoration using extracted features of the damaged image. This paper instead develops an approach that starts reverse diffusion from the raw low-quality image, motivated by a theoretical argument for that choice.

The proposed P-I2SB framework uses a Schrödinger bridge to learn transport between image distributions. The authors identify optimality and reversibility issues in existing bridge solutions that lead to suboptimal restoration. Their central modification happens during training: high-quality images are transformed into pseudo-samples using a hashing rule related to the low-quality images, making the distributions structurally similar.

The paper states that this distribution correction guarantees optimal and reversible bridge solutions, enabling the restoration process to learn effectively. Reported results reach state-of-the-art blind face restoration performance, with more natural textures while retaining inference speed relative to previous methods. The approach thus connects how training distributions are prepared with how effectively a model can restore directly from the degraded image.
icml-2025-feature-out-let-raw-image-as-y.tldr: P-I2SB reshapes training image distributions to support theoretically optimal, reversible bridge solutions for restoring faces directly from degraded images.

paragraphs: A graph model may encounter a sequence of domains whose distributions differ from its earlier training data. Adapting once to a single new domain does not address this continuing change, and repeated adaptation can erase earlier knowledge. GCAL tackles the combined problem of learning from new graph domains while retaining useful information from previous ones.

Its bilevel optimization links two phases. During adaptation, an information-maximization objective fine-tunes the model on new domains while also re-adapting stored memories. During memory generation, a variational graph-generation module condenses original graphs into memory graphs. A theoretical lower bound derived from information bottleneck theory guides this compression process.

These components give the method a way to revisit earlier domains through condensed graph representations while continuing to adapt. The reported experiments show substantial improvements over existing methods in both adaptability and knowledge retention. The results support treating memory construction and domain adaptation as connected learning problems, particularly when distribution shifts continue across multiple graphs instead of ending after a single transition.
icml-2025-gcal-adapting-graph-models-to-.tldr: GCAL jointly adapts graph models and generates compact graph memories to improve learning across continuing domain shifts.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning trains graph neural networks collaboratively while keeping data local. Restricting communication to one round can help in resource-limited settings, but it removes the repeated exchanges that many methods rely on. A global model must then combine knowledge from diverse graph structures without gradual rounds of personalized refinement.

GHOST creates a proxy model for each client and uses those proxies to integrate local knowledge into global training. It also identifies and consolidates parameters that are important for representing graph topology. This second component addresses a problem caused by strong local structural biases: training can overfit particular client distributions and forget useful structural knowledge.

The framework therefore couples a mechanism for collecting diverse client knowledge with one for retaining it during integration. Experiments on real-world tasks report superior performance and generalization. These findings support proxy-based knowledge integration as an approach to one-shot federated graph learning, where efficient communication must be balanced with the global model's ability to handle graph structures beyond any individual client's local distribution.
icml-2025-ghost-generalizable-one-shot-f.tldr: GHOST combines client proxy models and topology-preserving parameter consolidation to improve one-shot federated graph learning.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, sharing one policy network lets agents pool learning experience efficiently. However, identical shared parameters can also encourage overly similar behavior. This paper traces part of that problem to gradient conflicts: different agents can request opposing changes to the same neuron, causing their updates to cancel.

GradPS identifies these ineffective, or futile, neurons and dynamically creates multiple copies. Agents with relatively compatible gradients share a copy, so their updates can still contribute jointly to learning. Separate copies can receive independent updates, giving agents room to develop different behaviors without abandoning parameter sharing throughout the entire network.

This makes the sharing arrangement responsive to where learning conflicts actually occur. It preserves the benefit of shared gradients within compatible groups while allowing differentiation where shared updates interfere. Extensive experiments show that GradPS learns diverse policies with promising performance. The stated findings support gradient conflict as a useful signal for deciding which neurons should remain shared and which should be separated.
icml-2025-gradps-resolving-futile-neuron.tldr: GradPS clones neurons whose agent gradients conflict, retaining useful parameter sharing while enabling more diverse policies.

paragraphs: Training a diffusion model across multiple workers introduces differences in computing capacity and available data. Theory built around a single worker may assume accurate estimation of the score function used by the model. The paper examines how resource limitations and data diversity challenge that assumption when training is distributed.

The authors derive a generation-error bound for distributed diffusion models in resource-limited environments. The bound depends linearly on data dimension and is consistent with established single-worker results. This provides a mathematical connection between distributed training and the simpler setting already studied, while explicitly addressing workers that cannot all contribute equally capable estimation.

The analysis also highlights how hyperparameter choices influence training dynamics and, through them, generation performance. Its main contribution is a theoretical framework for reasoning about distributed diffusion training under unequal resources and data availability. The linear dependence describes the derived error bound, rather than an empirical claim that every increase in dimension causes an exactly proportional deterioration in generated samples.
icml-2025-how-distributed-collaboration-.tldr: The paper derives a generation-error bound for resource-limited distributed diffusion training and analyzes the importance of hyperparameter choices.

paragraphs: As new data arrives, a learning system must decide whether each sample or batch is worth annotating and learning from. Keeping everything can waste labeling and training effort. Info-Coevolution addresses this decision online, allowing dataset construction and model improvement to proceed together instead of automatically absorbing all available data.

The framework uses task-specific models, along with open-source models, to select and annotate incoming or web data. The authors describe the selection process as avoiding bias. An important feature is that the amount of data saved emerges automatically from the process, without requiring a manually tuned saving ratio.

On real-world datasets including ImageNet-1K, the method reduces annotation and training costs by 32% without losing performance. Combined with semi-supervised learning, it reduces the annotation ratio to 50%. The paper also explores improving datasets through retrieval from unlabeled open-source data. These findings support selective dataset growth as a practical way to reduce redundant work while keeping model performance intact in the reported evaluations.
icml-2025-info-coevolution-an-efficient-.tldr: Info-Coevolution selectively annotates incoming data, reducing reported annotation and training costs by 32% without performance loss.

paragraphs: Continual instruction tuning updates a large model as successive instruction datasets arrive. Ordinary gradient updates can substantially damage performance on earlier datasets. Averaging current and previous parameters can reduce forgetting, but a fixed averaging weight may not balance preservation and adaptation appropriately when the incoming data keeps changing.

The paper develops a framework around an ideal condition for this balance between stability and plasticity. Using a Taylor expansion of the loss, the authors derive a balance weight determined by gradients and learned parameters. The resulting coefficient adapts the parameter update to reduce interference between existing knowledge and new learning.

The framework also uses semantic similarity between instructions to decide whether to retrain parameters or expand the trainable parameter set. At test time, instruction similarity helps allocate suitable parameters to each instance. Across multiple continual instruction-tuning benchmarks, experiments show reduced forgetting and improved overall performance. The contribution combines an adaptive update rule with decisions about which parameters should learn and serve different instructions.
icml-2025-large-continual-instruction-as.tldr: An adaptive parameter-averaging coefficient and instruction-based parameter allocation improve continual instruction tuning and reduce forgetting.

paragraphs: Fine-grained open-set detection asks a model to recognize unfamiliar classes that closely resemble familiar ones. A class hierarchy can expose subtle relationships among known categories, potentially helping distinguish an unknown category even when it shares a parent with known categories. The challenge is to turn that hierarchy into an effective learning representation.

The paper argues that placing a separate detector at each hierarchy node and proceeding from top to bottom can perform poorly. Its theoretical analysis also finds that directly maximizing the probability of the path to the correct leaf leads to a suboptimal training process. Simply adding hierarchical decisions therefore does not resolve the learning problem.

The proposed alternative represents nodes through a state space constructed from the entire hierarchy. The authors prove that this state-based representation guarantees maximization of the probability along the correct leaf's path. The distinction is between directly optimizing that path objective and obtaining the property through the proposed representation. Experiments on multiple real-world hierarchical datasets report superior detection performance, supporting the value of modeling the hierarchy as a whole.
icml-2025-learning-state-based-node-repr.tldr: State-based representations built from a whole class hierarchy improve detection of unfamiliar classes that closely resemble known ones.

paragraphs: Vector quantization represents information through discrete entries in a codebook. This gives neural networks discrete latent representations, but choosing discrete entries prevents standard backpropagation through that choice. The resulting difficulty is not just learning an encoder and decoder; it is also training a codebook that serves their task effectively.

Meta-Quantization separates codebook optimization and autoencoder optimization into two levels, drawing on meta-learning. It replaces a codebook directly parameterized by embeddings with a hyper-network that generates the codebook dynamically from autoencoder feedback. The resulting meta-objective makes codebook learning responsive to the task performed by the surrounding model.

This design changes how the discrete representation is learned: feedback from the autoencoder helps determine the codebook itself. The authors evaluate the framework in VQVAE and VQGAN architectures on image reconstruction and generation. Reported experiments show superior generative performance, supporting Meta-Quantization as a potential alternative to existing vector-quantization methods. The evidence described concerns these image tasks, while the motivation includes the broader usefulness of discrete representations.
icml-2025-learning-to-quantize-for-train.tldr: Meta-Quantization dynamically generates task-aware codebooks through two-level optimization and improves reported image-generation performance.

paragraphs: Image watermarking models need to embed recoverable information without visibly damaging an image. Large models can perform well but are costly to deploy, while smaller ones may sacrifice robustness or invisibility. This paper attributes part of that tradeoff to training losses that encourage optimization in directions irrelevant to the actual decoding goal.

The authors introduce two complementary remedies. A decoding-oriented surrogate loss reduces the influence of those irrelevant directions. A detachable projection head absorbs them during training and is removed for inference. They also design a watermarking framework with five submodules whose parameter counts can be reduced independently, creating additional control over model size.

The reported model improves efficiency, invisibility, and robustness while using only 2.2% of the parameters of the compared state-of-the-art frameworks. This supports the paper's central argument that better alignment between training and decoding can reduce parameter redundancy. The loss and projection-head methods are designed for plug-and-play use, so the contribution includes training components intended to support future lightweight watermarking architectures.
icml-2025-lightweight-mark-rethinking-de.tldr: Lightweight-Mark aligns training with watermark decoding and reports improved performance using only 2.2% of the parameters of compared leading frameworks.

paragraphs: This paper studies backdoors in diffusion bridge models that operate on complex input distributions, including image-to-image tasks. Earlier formulations largely focused on single attacks and models starting from Gaussian noise. MixBridge extends the research setting to arbitrary input distributions and multiple heterogeneous triggers within a unified diffusion Schrödinger bridge framework.

The authors show that poisoned image pairs can introduce backdoor behavior without modifying the model's stochastic differential equations. They also identify a theoretical obstacle to combining objectives in one bridge: the model follows a geometric mean of benign and backdoored distributions, creating conflicts among backdoor tasks. This explains why accommodating several triggers is not a straightforward extension of a single-trigger setting.

Their Divide-and-Merge strategy trains bridges separately for individual objectives and then combines them into one model. A weight-reallocation component is intended to make the resulting backdoors less conspicuous. Experiments across diverse generation tasks report that the framework is effective. The paper's contribution is both an analysis of conflicting bridge objectives and a framework for studying multiple backdoor behaviors in these generative models.
icml-2025-mixbridge-heterogeneous-image-.tldr: MixBridge studies multiple backdoors in diffusion bridge models and uses separately trained bridges to address conflicts among their objectives.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can transfer beyond its training distribution, but it can also learn spurious relationships that break under distribution shifts. This paper examines mini-batch construction as one plausible explanation for its generalization behavior. A causal analysis then connects learned spurious correlations to reduced out-of-distribution performance.

The authors define a post-intervention distribution using a structural causal model. Under this distribution, the spurious variable and label variable are independent. They show that if every training mini-batch satisfies this distribution, the resulting self-supervised model can achieve optimal worst-case out-of-distribution performance. The batch-level condition is central to the theoretical statement.

To turn that result into a training strategy, the paper learns a latent-variable model and uses it to sample batches subject to the proposed constraints. Theoretical analysis establishes identifiability of the latent model and supports the sampling method, while experiments on downstream out-of-distribution tasks show its effectiveness. The approach makes data grouping during training an explicit means of reducing reliance on misleading correlations.
icml-2025-on-the-out-of-distribution-gen.tldr: A causally motivated batch-sampling strategy reduces spurious correlations in self-supervised learning and improves reported out-of-distribution performance.

paragraphs: Decentralized unlearning seeks to remove one client's influence from an entire collaborative learning system. This is difficult because influence can travel through indirect connections, and the communication network can change over time. Repeating training to remove a client becomes especially difficult to scale when those connections are dynamic.

PDUDT provides an unlearning algorithm that requires neither additional communication nor retraining. Its theoretical guarantee compares the result with perturbed retraining: the two are statistically indistinguishable. This specifies the reference procedure for the guarantee, rather than claiming that the resulting parameters must be identical to those from an ordinary retraining run.

The authors also show that subsequent learning converges at order 1/T, where T counts communication rounds, matching state-of-the-art rates. Experiments report more than 99% less unlearning time than the Retrain method while achieving comparable unlearning performance. Together, these results address both the immediate cost of removing a client's influence and the system's ability to continue learning afterward under changing network connections.
icml-2025-pdudt-provable-decentralized-u.tldr: PDUDT removes a client's influence without extra communication or retraining, with a perturbed-retraining guarantee and over 99% reported time savings.

paragraphs: Federated distillation exchanges model outputs such as logits to transfer knowledge between clients and a server. This can accommodate clients with different architectures and data distributions while keeping communication lightweight. The paper identifies temperature calibration, which controls distillation intensity, as a bottleneck in combining that knowledge effectively.

ReT-FHD adjusts temperatures at two levels. Its elastic mechanism changes distillation intensity across model layers, while a global category-aware mechanism calibrates individual classes using confidence distributions in global logits. These components make knowledge transfer sensitive to both where information occurs in a model and which class is being considered. A blockchain-verified validation component, Z-Score Guard, adds protection against malicious contributions.

Across benchmarks with varying data and model heterogeneity, the framework reports significant accuracy improvements and substantially reduced communication costs. The abstract also reports mitigation of 44% of label-flipping and model-poisoning attacks. The findings support carefully calibrated logits as sufficient knowledge carriers for the studied heterogeneous federated systems, with the reported attack mitigation representing partial protection.
icml-2025-rethinking-the-temperature-for.tldr: ReT-FHD adapts distillation temperatures across layers and classes to improve heterogeneous federated learning, with an added attack-validation mechanism.

paragraphs: Multi-view subspace clustering groups unlabeled samples using multiple representations of the same data. Anchors reduce computational cost, but their quality and robustness affect the resulting groups. RCSC jointly learns shared anchors, the graph connecting samples to them, and the graph partition, so these components can improve one another during optimization.

The paper first establishes a conditional structural result: with sufficiently sampled independent subspaces and suitable objective-function conditions, the learned anchor graph is block diagonal. Its concrete model combines a Frobenius-norm objective with nonnegative and affine constraints. A geometric analysis explains how these ingredients restrict sample representations according to local cluster distributions in affine subspaces.

RCSC also uses correlations among consensus anchors to encourage related anchors to group together, guided by projections specific to each view. An alternating optimization strategy solves the unified objective. Experiments on eight multi-view datasets report superior effectiveness and efficiency. The theoretical result explains when cleanly separated graph structure can arise, while the empirical findings support jointly learning robust anchors and clusters on the evaluated datasets.
icml-2025-robust-consensus-anchor-learni.tldr: RCSC jointly learns robust shared anchors and clusters, with conditional guarantees for separated graph structure and strong results on eight datasets.

paragraphs: An ensemble's behavior depends on how much weight it assigns to each constituent model. Choosing those weights using validation data can work poorly when future data follows a different distribution. Structure-informed Risk Minimization addresses this problem by learning ensemble weights for robustness without using test data.

The framework draws on distributionally robust optimization, which evaluates performance over a set of possible distributions. SRM shapes this uncertainty set using structural information from training distributions, rather than relying only on divergence measures. The aim is to focus robustness on plausible shifts and reduce the excessive pessimism that can arise when optimizing against an overly broad worst case.

The authors provide a computationally efficient optimization algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Across diverse benchmarks, SRM achieves better out-of-distribution generalization than existing ensemble-combination strategies. The findings support using distribution structure when deciding how models should be combined: robustness depends not only on optimizing against uncertainty, but also on making that uncertainty set reflect the kinds of changes the method is intended to handle.
icml-2025-structure-informed-risk-minimi.tldr: SRM learns robust ensemble weights by using training-distribution structure to focus worst-case optimization on plausible distribution shifts.

paragraphs: The paper proposes that interactions between people and language models can form a reinforcing feedback loop. Models learn beliefs from human-produced data, generate content that reinforces those beliefs, and later absorb the reinforced beliefs through further data. Repetition could make existing views harder to dislodge and reduce the diversity of ideas.

The authors call this the lock-in hypothesis and formalize it for empirical study. They examine it using both simulations with language-model agents and real-world GPT usage data. Combining these forms of evidence lets them investigate the proposed feedback mechanism alongside patterns observed in actual model use.

Their analysis finds abrupt declines in diversity after releases of new GPT iterations, with those declines persisting afterward. The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with the hypothesized feedback loop. The stated conclusion retains an important distinction: sustained diversity losses support the hypothesis, while entrenchment of false beliefs remains a potential consequence. The paper frames human-model interaction as a process whose repeated cycles may shape the range of ideas people encounter and preserve.
icml-2025-the-lock-in-hypothesis-stagnat.tldr: The paper finds sustained diversity declines consistent with a hypothesis that human–LLM feedback loops can entrench existing beliefs.

paragraphs: Continual learning updates a model as tasks arrive sequentially while trying to retain earlier knowledge. For large pretrained models, this must also be computationally affordable. TreeLoRA addresses that combination by constructing low-rank adapters separately across layers, guided by a hierarchy of similarities between task gradients.

The gradient-similarity tree gives the method a structured way to use relationships among tasks when building adapters. Estimating those relationships can itself be expensive, so the authors introduce a bandit-based algorithm using lower confidence bounds to explore task structure efficiently. Sparse gradient updates further reduce the burden of parameter optimization.

The paper supplies theoretical analysis supporting the approach and evaluates it with vision transformers and large language models. Experiments across vision and natural-language tasks demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution brings together three related decisions: how to organize task relationships, how to estimate those relationships economically, and how to update parameters sparsely. That combination targets the cost of continual adaptation as well as the need to preserve earlier learning.
icml-2025-treelora-efficient-continual-l.tldr: TreeLoRA uses a hierarchy of task-gradient similarities, bandit exploration, and sparse updates for efficient continual adaptation of large models.

paragraphs: This paper studies deep Q-networks in a continuous-time decision-making framework. It connects reinforcement learning to stochastic control through forward-backward stochastic differential equations. The analysis considers a continuous-time Markov decision process driven by a square-integrable martingale, making that mathematical setting part of the scope of its approximation results.

Within this framework, the authors show that deep Q-networks can approximate the optimal Q-function arbitrarily accurately on compact sets with high probability. They combine residual-network approximation results with large-deviation bounds for the state-action process. They also analyze convergence of a general Q-learning training algorithm by adapting stochastic approximation theorems.

The analysis highlights how network depth interacts with time discretization. It also uses viscosity-solution ideas, primarily for the optimal value function, to address possible nonsmoothness of the optimal Q-function. These results provide a theoretical bridge between network representation and continuous-time control. Their relevance to physical systems and high-frequency data comes from studying decisions in continuous time, with the guarantees tied to the stated mathematical setting.
icml-2025-universal-approximation-theore.tldr: In a specified continuous-time setting, deep Q-networks can approximate optimal Q-functions arbitrarily accurately on compact sets with high probability.

paragraphs: A generated video can look convincing while still being unsuitable for guiding an embodied agent. WorldSimBench addresses the need to evaluate predictive video models from both perspectives. The paper first organizes predictive-model capabilities into a hierarchy, then introduces a dual evaluation framework for models intended to function as world simulators.

The perceptual component assesses visual fidelity using human preferences. The authors introduce HF-Embodied, a video-assessment dataset containing fine-grained human feedback, and use it to train a preference evaluator aligned with human perception. This provides an explicit measure of how generated videos appear to human viewers.

The manipulative component evaluates consistency between generated video and actions: it asks whether situation-aware predictions can be translated into correct control signals in dynamic environments. The benchmark covers open-ended embodied environments, autonomous driving, and robot manipulation. Together, the two evaluations examine both visual quality and usefulness for control. The paper presents the benchmark and its evaluation as a foundation for improving world simulators, rather than treating visual fidelity alone as evidence of embodied capability.
icml-2025-worldsimbench-towards-video-ge.tldr: WorldSimBench evaluates video world simulators through both human judgments of visual quality and consistency with embodied control actions.
